title: Durable reactive CO2 capture exceeding 1,000 h via self-reinforcing molecular catalysts - Nature Energy
gist: Nature Energy paper (abstract only available) shows a covalently linked cobalt phthalocyanine catalyst on carbon nanotubes sustains reactive CO2 capture-and-conversion to CO for over 1,000 h at 50 mA cm-2, by turning early Co leaching into a self-stabilizing vacancy network. Shell Global Solutions co-authored and funded the work.

insights.claim: Reactive CO2 capture integrates capture and electrochemical conversion and avoids the energy-intensive desorption/regeneration step needed to produce high-purity CO2, but existing systems have poor durability.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Durability, not efficiency, is the gating factor for integrated capture-and-conversion to commercialize.

insights.claim: The pH swing intrinsic to reactive-capture systems drives protons toward the cathode, creating an acidic microenvironment that accelerates demetallation of molecular catalysts.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific degradation mechanism that catalyst developers in this field must design against.

insights.claim: In a covalently linked cobalt phthalocyanine catalyst on carbon nanotubes, an early loss of about 50% of the Co generates vacancies that make neighbouring Co sites contract, strengthening Co-N coordination and suppressing further demetallation.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive route to stability: sacrificial metal loss improves the remaining catalyst, so loading and stability trade-offs may be rethought.

insights.claim: The catalyst ran continuously for over 1,000 h at 50 mA cm-2 with about 80% CO Faradaic efficiency and 39% energy efficiency at 2.9 V.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The 1,000 h benchmark sets a bar for reactive-capture durability; 39% energy efficiency at 2.9 V still shows room for improvement before commercial use.

insights.claim: Shell Global Solutions International B.V. funded the study and Shell staff are among the authors, alongside the University of Toronto (Sinton group), University of Queensland, and National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Signals oil-major interest in electrochemical CO2-to-CO conversion paired with carbon capture.

insights.claim: The paper positions robust molecular catalysts as a pathway to decarbonize chemical and fuel production using low-carbon electricity via CO2 reduction.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Economics depend on cheap clean power; watch electrolyzer cost and power prices for CO-route chemicals.
